slides.title: AI in IT operations
slides.subtitle: The emerging role of a decision model
slides.notes: A discussion document, not an investment request. One example of a decision model, TypeSafe's Jev, makes the idea concrete; the argument is about the decision layer, not the vendor.

slides.title: AI is entering incident work, one capability at a time
slides.subtitle: Applications already interpret, coordinate and connect context; the decision is what remains
items: Observability platforms already interpret signals: Dynatrace's Davis correlates anomalies and points to a root cause, and Datadog's Bits AI SRE investigates incidents from operational evidence.
Service-management platforms coordinate the workflow: ServiceNow documents agents for alert assignment, analysis and verification.
Cloud and network tooling connect context to response: AWS DevOps Agent draws on telemetry, code and deployment data, while F5 exposes device, VIP and pool context.
slides.notes: Vendor-reported examples, to show the direction of travel, not to rank products. Interpretation is moving into the tools already in the estate.

slides.title: Each platform starts from a different position, and none completes the cycle
slides.subtitle: Selected examples; the categories overlap
headers: What it brings to the workflow
rows: Tickets, ownership, process; the broadest coverage
slides.takeaway: ServiceNow covers the most of the cycle, but it can be expensive and slow to customise - which is where lighter, specialised components earn a place.
slides.notes: An illustrative market map, not a ranking. ServiceNow is placed as the broadest single platform; the note on cost and customisation is widely reported and worth testing against the licence in place.

slides.title: Think end to end: the cycle from Detect to Learn, and where custom components fit
slides.subtitle: A conceptual view of the workflow
slides.body: Platforms and tools already automate detection, correlation, execution and record-keeping well. The links in the middle - interpretation, ownership, severity, and the act-or-page call - are where a small custom decision component can fit, without replacing anything around it.
slides.notes: A conceptual simplification, not a claim that every workflow is linear. Rule-based detection and numerical checks remain valuable. The proposal is interpretation of supplied context at the decision links only.

slides.title: The Jev opportunity: a decision model that fits those links
slides.subtitle: What it is, and why it is worth a look
left: TypeSafe's Jev: a 'System One' decision model, not a chat model
In: one request with a state (the alert and its context) and a set of typed questions
Out: a typed answer to each question, with a probability
Three question types: Choice (pick from a list), Score (place on a scale) and Noul (the probability that a statement is true)
slides.right_title: Why it is worth a look
right: The questions are yours, and so are the thresholds
Ordinary code compares the probabilities with those thresholds and decides what happens
One call answers many questions in milliseconds, at a fraction of a cent of inference
The open question: are the answers accurate enough on your tickets?
slides.notes: The honest case for a test, not a claim of superiority. The model answers what it is asked; it does not discover telemetry. Choice and Score expose confidence and probability distributions, which need evaluation on the task. Compare against current rules and simple alternatives.

slides.title: How this looks today, by hand - and with a decision step
slides.subtitle: The same incident, before and after

before.title: Today, by hand
steps: Opens the dashboards and the logs
Judges how bad it is and whether to act
outcome: Minutes to hours, and the answer depends on who is on call and how busy the shift is

after.title: With a decision step
steps: The platform sends the alert and its context to one call
It returns the classification, the severity and a proposed action, each with a probability
Ordinary code applies thresholds you own
It either acts or asks a person
outcome: The same questions, answered the same way, every time

slides.notes: The manual column is a description of common practice, not a measurement. The decision step does not remove the engineer; it removes the repeated reading and judging, and leaves the judgement calls it is not sure about to a person.

slides.title: An example, end to end: a service becomes unreachable
slides.subtitle: One recorded example from the project's set; the gate's checks with signed margins
slides.takeaway: A name-resolution failure is read once and classified as a network incident; the gate either permits an action or sends it to a person, with every check and its margin recorded.
slides.source: Our measurement | one recorded example | gate checks from zeroops/policy.py
slides.notes: Network incidents are reported by tools like F5 in several common shapes: a pool member failing its health check, a virtual server unreachable, a certificate expiring on a VIP, or an HA failover. The example here uses a name-resolution failure (a service unreachable) because it is text-rich and decision-friendly; a certificate expiry is the same four calls. In practice the platform's own checks and topology stay where they are; the model only answers the typed questions from the text it is given.

slides.title: The same call, question by question
slides.subtitle: Twelve typed questions, answered in one request
slides.body: This is one call. The state sent is the alert and its context - the service or VIP, recent changes, and the relevant log lines. The questions are fixed, and every answer comes back with a probability. The gate reads only the answers it needs.
slides.notes: One request returns every answer; adding questions adds little latency. This is why a network incident and an application incident can share one decision step: the questions are fixed and the context varies. Each answer carries a probability, so the gate can act, ask a person, or log.

slides.title: The same call, running end to end
slides.subtitle: The technical component: the contract, the primitives and the gate, in motion
slides.body: The demo sends the same request through the contract, the three primitives and the gate. Nothing is scripted: the typed output and the gate decide each outcome, and the run ends on the same network incident used earlier.
slides.notes: Play the embedded video (2:03) in the slide. It walks one request through the call, the three primitives (Choice, Score, Noul), and the gate that turns a typed answer and a threshold into an action. It is the technical counterpart to the example slides, not a summary.

slides.title: All four models worked; the differences are modest
slides.subtitle: The same questions, answered by four models
slides.takeaway: Every model answered sensibly, and none automated a case labelled unsafe. The point is that a typed decision step is workable - not which model wins.
slides.notes: Read the caveats with the table: the {n} incidents reduce to {templates} templates; root cause scored high because the clues are explicit; the acceptable-action list was written after the first run; and {rollback_proposed} of the proposed actions were rollback, the first option offered, against {rollback_labelled} labels. Accuracy and margins on real tickets are untested.

slides.title: How it integrates with the software you already run
slides.subtitle: One call from the tools in place; nothing is replaced
blocks: F5 · Dynatrace · ServiceNow alerts, tickets, context
Thresholds you own decide act, ask, or log
slides.body: Documented integration points exist for common COTS software: ServiceNow (IntegrationHub REST step or MID Server script), PagerDuty (Event Orchestration rules, Custom Event Transformers, webhooks) and F5 (iRules or telemetry). A fixed flow acts on the answers and falls back to existing rules on timeout or low confidence.
slides.notes: Latency inside that stack, under rate limits and during an incident storm, is untested. The enterprise keeps its connectors, data access and execution controls; the model is a bounded call inside the existing workflow.

slides.title: Why a decision model is attractive: versatile, easy to configure, low cost
slides.subtitle: The properties to weigh against the platform's own AI
levers: One interface covers classification, severity, routing and yes/no checks, across application and network incidents.
Questions and thresholds are written in code - no prompt engineering and no model training to start.
A fraction of a cent of inference per incident; the real cost is integration and ownership.
Milliseconds per call, and ordinary code holds the thresholds and the decision.
slides.body: Flexibility and cost sit on one side; data handling, integration and the effort of ownership sit on the other. That is the trade to weigh against what the platform already provides.
slides.notes: These are properties of the approach, not measured business results. Low inference cost does not remove integration, evaluation and maintenance work, and a shared component needs a named owner.

slides.title: How to explore this together: size the opportunity, then a staged pilot
slides.subtitle: Three short stages, each ending in a decision

steps.name: Diagnostic
does: Baseline reassignment, triage and out-of-hours volume
Check what the current licence already does
steps.decision: Is there a gap worth closing?

steps.name: Offline replay
does: Run 2,000-5,000 closed tickets through the same questions
Compare the answers with current rules
steps.decision: Does it beat what runs today, by enough to matter?

steps.name: Shadow, then assist
does: Shadow: answers go to hidden fields; no action is taken
Assist: answers become suggestions; overrides are tracked

help: Bring this harness, the question design and the gate
Work alongside your platform and data teams
Support the compliance and operating-model calls
slides.notes: Durations and criteria are judgement, not measured results. The harness runs any model, so the choice of tool stays with the organisation. Thresholds should not be tuned on the data used to claim final performance.

slides.title: Twelve considerations that decide whether this fits an estate
slides.subtitle: Short titles; full text in outputs/3_open-questions-and-next-steps.md
rows: It fits text classification at volume, and little else
The value is the gap to what you already run
Results depend on what the ticket says at the moment of decision
Thresholds and calibration must come from your own data
Question wording and option order shape the answer
Anyone who can write into a ticket can lean on the answer
The gate is only as good as what it checks and how it fails
The vendor is young, hosted in one region, and the model moves
The API call is the easy part of the integration
Inference is almost free; people and alternatives decide the economics
Regulatory duties depend on how each use is classified
Someone has to own the questions, the thresholds and on-call trust
slides.notes: The full text, sources and labels for each consideration are in the questions document; this is a reference for diligence.

slides.title: Risks, security and compliance, and how each could be contained
slides.subtitle: The conditions a real test would manage
rows: Adversarial text in tickets or logs can move an answer
Keep untrusted text out of questions that gate actions; keep action authority outside the model
Shuffle option order and repeat; set thresholds on held-out data
Thresholds and calibration are unproven on our data
Choose thresholds on held-out tickets; re-run after each model release
Vendor is young; model moves under an alias; no EU region
Pin the version; redaction and a signed DPA; start in shadow mode
Log input hash, model version, option order, probabilities and threshold version; take legal review
slides.notes: EU AI Act duties depend on how each use is classified; the general case in the research overstates it, so check current guidance. The independent review documents injection and option-order effects; severity depends on the task.

slides.title: Open or proprietary: both work; the trade-off is control against convenience
slides.subtitle: The decision layer can be hosted or run in your environment
items: Adopt quickly and operate nothing; the trade-off is that incident text leaves your environment, under a signed DPA and zero-retention terms.
Run it inside your network with no data egress; you own the GPUs, fine-tuning and upkeep, and untuned accuracy starts lower.
Either can serve as the decision layer. This project's harness runs any model, so the choice can follow data-residency and operating preferences.
slides.notes: A balanced view on purpose: hosted options are fast and low-effort, open options give control and privacy at the cost of operations and tuning. Neither is claimed to be more accurate in general.

slides.title: About Jev and TypeSafe
slides.subtitle: What is known about the model used as the example, as of October 2026
rows: TypeSafe AI, San Francisco; Jev entered early access in September 2026
Jev, marketed as a 'System One' decision model: not a chat model, and it does not generate text
One REST call: a state in; typed answers with probabilities out
Choice (pick from a list), Score (place on a scale), Noul (probability a statement is true)
Hosted API in one region; input tokens billed, output free (list about $0.042 per million input tokens)
Young and moving; this project pins the version (jev-1.13.0) and re-validates after each release
slides.notes: Vendor-reported facts, not independently audited. No named production IT-operations customer was found in the research; treat availability, rate limits and compliance terms as unsettled and confirm them with the vendor before any real ticket is sent.
